content: In medical terms, quickening refers to the first moment a pregnant woman perceives or feels the movement of the fetus within her uterus. The Oxford English Dictionary defines to quicken as reaching the stage of pregnancy where the fetus shows signs of life. With the advent of ultrasound technology in the 20th century, it became possible to observe fetal movements even before the pregnant woman could feel them. This technological advancement has added complexity to the concept of quickening. The initial sensation of quickening is often described as a light tapping or a fluttering feeling, similar to the movement of a butterfly. As the pregnancy progresses, these sensations become stronger and more regular. Early fetal movements are sometimes mistaken for gas or hunger pangs. The uterine muscles, rather than the abdominal muscles, are the first to detect fetal motion. Consequently, a woman’s body weight does not significantly influence when these movements are first perceived. Women who have previously given birth tend to have more relaxed uterine muscles, which are more sensitive to fetal motion. For these women, fetal movements can sometimes be felt as early as 14 weeks into the pregnancy. Typically, quickening occurs naturally around the midpoint of pregnancy. For a multiparous woman (one who has had previous pregnancies), fetal movements are usually felt around 18 weeks. Historically, the term quick originally meant alive. Quickening has sometimes been regarded as the point at which the fetus begins to possess individual life. In the 18th century, British legal scholar William Blackstone discussed quickening in the context of feticide and abortion. However, quickening was only one of several historical standards used to determine when the right to life attaches to a fetus. According to ancient law, as described by Blackstone, another standard was the formation of the fetus, which occurs weeks before quickening. Henry Bracton, writing about 500 years before Blackstone, also referenced this ancient law. The idea that a fetus was considered alive upon formation dates back at least another millennium before Bracton. For instance, in the Septuagint text of the Old Testament, killing a fetus was considered taking a life if the fetus was perfectly formed. Thus, the perception of quickening by a pregnant woman has historically been only one of several markers used to determine when human life legally begins. Other markers have included viability, birth, and conception. In the 18th and 19th centuries, a woman convicted of a capital crime could request a delay in her execution if she was pregnant. However, in Ireland in 1831, Baron Pennefather ruled that pregnancy alone was insufficient for such a delay; quickening had to be established.
